title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: What did IBM do when the consolidated service platform saw no uptake? `[V]`
options: Ran a change-management campaign and extended the transition period
Shut off the HR email address and phone line, and told around 21,000 managers their HR partners were no longer available for routine questions
Made self-service mandatory for a pilot population before scaling
Rebuilt the platform based on user feedback before relaunching
questions.explanation: Removing the alternative is the decision the case turns on, and it is the one most organizations won't take. A and D are the moves that feel responsible and leave the old channel intact, which is why uptake doesn't change.

questions.prompt: What is the correct characterization of the −35 figure? `[V]`
options: Employee Net Promoter Score for the company overall
An internal customer-satisfaction score for the HR service — not eNPS, which is how it is usually misquoted
The percentage decline in HR service usage during the transition
A composite index of satisfaction and resolution time
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the fall is real and the metric is a service score. The distinction matters for an audience that knows exactly what eNPS is and what −35 would mean on it.

questions.prompt: What does the J-curve say about the trough?
options: That it can be avoided with sufficient change management
That it indicates a design flaw that should be corrected before proceeding
That service genuinely does get worse, and that this is the shape of the transition rather than evidence of failure
That its depth is proportional to the size of the population affected
questions.explanation: The important word is *genuinely*. It isn't a perception problem to be communicated away: people really can't find things, and edge cases really do fall through, until habit forms.

questions.prompt: What does the module identify as the binding constraint on a transformation like this?
options: The quality of the self-service technology
The sponsor's tolerance for the trough
The change-management resource available
The size of the operating budget being targeted
questions.explanation: Almost every failure happens at the same place: month four, numbers at their worst, complaints escalated, somebody senior proposing a pause.

questions.prompt: Why is pausing at the bottom of a J-curve described as the worst available move?
options: Because restarting requires a new business case
Because it guarantees the full cost of the disruption without any of the benefit, and teaches the organization that these initiatives get abandoned when they get hard
Because the technology investment is typically non-refundable
Because staff who were redeployed cannot be returned to their original roles
questions.explanation: The second half is the expensive part: it raises the cost of the next attempt by everyone, not just yours.

questions.prompt: What is the sequencing rule, and why does the module say it is practical rather than moral?
options: That transformations should begin with the smallest function; because risk is contained

That you have no standing to tell another function to redesign until you have done it to your own; because the question they will ask is what it actually costs, and only a practitioner can answer that
That HR must complete its own transformation before the technology is available elsewhere
That functions should transform in order of their exposure to automation
questions.explanation: And it is also the answer to Module 3: the scope fight is won by demonstrated competence, and this is the demonstration.

questions.prompt: Why did IBM raise entry-level hiring while cutting the HR operating budget? `[V]`
options: To offset the reputational effect of the service consolidation
Because automating the work junior people used to do while also cutting junior hiring dries the well — in three to five years there is no mid-level population, because the entry point was removed
Because regulatory requirements mandated minimum graduate intake
Because entry-level roles were cheaper than the automation licences
questions.explanation: It is the least-quoted part of the case and the one that reframes it: the question isn't what you can cut but what the cut funds.

questions.prompt: A learner's honest answer is that the saving would be banked rather than reinvested. How should that be treated?
options: As a failure to apply the module, since reinvestment is required
As legitimate in some conditions, provided the write-up then addresses why the function should continue to be led by a CPO rather than run down
As acceptable only if paired with a commitment to reinvest in a later cycle
As evidence the cut was too large for the function to absorb
questions.explanation: Banking a saving is a real decision and sometimes the right one. What it isn't is a proposal that requires a CPO, which is a conclusion the learner should reach deliberately rather than back into.
